Something's Fishy - Rhodes Research on Vanderkloof Dam

By: Anina Peens | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A fishing scheme posing as a research project by Rhodes University at Vanderkloof Dam, is causing the further extinction of the Large Mouth Yellow fish and impoverishing the local fishing community

Unique Selling Point:
A dubious fishing project spearheaded by Rhodes University and funded with taxpayer’s money, is causing the extinction of the critically endangered Large Mouth Yellow fish in their last remaining habitat in Africa, the Vanderkloof dam.
The local impoverished fishing community around the dam that has been dependent on fishing for nearly half a century is also further being deprived of resources by the Rhodes project.


Summary:
A suspicious experimental fishing project at Vanderkloof dam, designed to assess the viability of a small-scale fisheries, is slowly causing the extinction of the globally endangered Large Mouthed Yellow fish (LMY). This, while the project that was designed to uplift the poor Northern Cape fishing communities, is now further impoverishing them. The state funded project implemented by Rhodes University seems to be a commercial operation under the guise of research. Tons of fish have been killed and no research data is being furnished to justify the project. The project is also adding to the collapse of the local tourism industry due to the use of illegal gillnets on South Africa’s second largest dam.

Further information:
The Large Mouthed Yellow fish is only found in the Orange and Vaal Systems but due to high level pollution in the Vaal river and dam, Vanderkloof dam is the last remaining habitat for this critically endangered species. Vanderkloof dam is also the bread and butter of the local fishing community. And yet, aware of these issues, Rhodes University has been granted permits by the Northern Cape department of Rural development, exempting them to use illegal gill nets in the dam for alleged research purposes. The project is now depleting the dam of its natural resources while there seems to be no control over the catch and killing of the Large Mouth Yellow fish. Since the project is facilitated by an academic institution, ethical clearance needs to be granted by the university involved to minimize risk to both human and animal involved during data collection. No ethical clearance was obtained at the onset of the project. When it started, the project made lavish promises to the desperately poor fishing communities around the dam who have been surviving on the fish resources for half a century. Since the project is funded by taxpayer’s money, it also committed to skills development for the fishermen. Various fishing methods were also to be explored in order to identify the best possible options when establishing a commercial fishery. After the experiment and skills development, the project was earmarked to be handed over to the local community. Yet, more than two years into the project, the same methods of fishing, which include the use of illegal gill nets, are still being used. The community is forced to buy the fish from the project and sell to the same markets to which the project also sells, at a discounted rate. The local fishermen have not benefited from the project at all.



Extra Budget Items:
Road travel suggested only

First interview in Cape Town: No travel or accommodation required.
Cape Town to Rhodes University in Grahamstown required- 870km - plus one night accommodation in Grahamstown for producer and camera operator. Camera operator travel costs from PE should be calculated.
Travel from Grahamstown to Vanderkloof Dam - 470km - One night accommodation in Vanderkloof Dam necessary for producer and camera operator. I have a good contact that is quite affordable. The same camera operator hailing from PE may be able to travel to VDK and back to PE.
Travel from Vanderkloof Dam to Johannesburg - 600km -local camera operator necessary, no accommodation required.



Case Study:
Lorenzo Damster Fisherman

Expert:
Mr. Gary Shun King Fish Scientist
Mrs. Elize Nel Former office manager
Mr. Qurban Rouhani Project leader
Mr. Jeremy Ridl Legal Advisor
Mr. Kishan Sankar Spokesperson; National Department of Fisheries

Locations:
CAPE TOWN & JOHANNESBURG
Grahamstown
Vanderkloof Dam- Northern Cape

Other Footage Sources:
Mainstreet Media has footage of the gill nets and the Rhodes project operating on the dam. It is unlikely that we will be able to capture this again. Mainstreet can also provide visuals of general fishing in the dam and cutaways of the dam, Vanderkloof town and surroundings.

Hidden Camera: No

Legal: Yes
Reason for legal: Qurban Rouhani has been dictating to me how the interview will take place and is restricting me from asking any follow up questions. He also does not want to appear on camera and wants to meet with me in person off the record. Since he is central to the project, he is a very important interviewee and I will need some advise on how to approach the situation. I will also need guidance in obtaining documentation from Rhodes University such as the ethical clearance certificate for the research as well as the data that has been collected thus far. Since the project is funded by the state, I would like Rhodes to disclose relevant financial documentation with regards to the project expenses. I have also asked them who their external auditors are but they do not want to disclose this.

Graphics: Yes
Reason for graphics: Map of Vanderkloof Dam to geographically explain location to viewers

Script:


SOMETHING’S FISHY_04 09 2020 RHODES Nr of Fish & MASIFUNIDSE OUT
2” at start
Gary extra byte added and a swish to PTC
Clarence out 5’35”
Elize 7’15” stretch the start extra words
Paragraph in at 8’01”

INTRO VO: The Vanderkloof dam is one of the longest dams on the African continent, stretching over 110km across the Northern Cape and Free state provinces, and is South Africa’s second largest dam. Its deep, long and narrow structure and pristine waters are home to the iconic Largemouth Yellow fish, a buzz word in recreational angling societies across the world.

PTC: The dam is one of the few remaining habitats for the endangered largemouth yellowfish that occurs in the Orange and Vaal river system. It is an extremely sensitive fish and pollution in the Vaal system means that Vanderkloof and the Orange river basin hold the last clean water for the species to survive in. But in this Dam, it now faces certain death if caught in a gill net.

VO: And that is exactly what is happening. Since 2018, Rhodes University has been doing a research project on the dam, using gill nets. And taxpayers are funding it.

VO: Although gill nets are not allowed to be used on a dam where an endangered species is supposed to be protected by the state, the Department of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries – known as DAFF – granted the project an exemption to use the nets.

This exemption came with strict conditions that needed to be observed by Rhodes in conducting the research. The research was mandated by the state to establish whether a commercial fishery is viable at the dam. Gill nets are amongst some of the fishing methods used in the blue print experiment that will inform the state on the best possible options when rolling out inland commercial fisheries countrywide.

VO: In an attempt to ensure that all parties affected by the research are heard, an Advisory Group was set up to guide the Rhodes research project, consisting of scientists, local and national government, fishermen, recreational anglers and civil society.

VO: Some members of the Advisory Group told us that they opposed the use of gill nets from the outset, but that Qurban Rouhani and Warwick Sauer, spearheading the research on behalf of Rhodes University, believed that research permit conditions ALLOWED the use of gill nets.

VO: Fish scientist Gary Shun King says using gill nets in Vanderkloof is like hunting antelope and hitting a couple of rhinos in the process.

ANINA QUESTION ON CAMERA:
“Gary you studied ichthyology at Rhodes University at the very same department that is implementing this project, why are you opposed to it?”

SUPER@ GARY SHUN KING, ICHTHYOLOGIST
“Anina, the damaging effects of gillnets can’t be underestimated. It is known worldwide. There are case studies that have been done all over Africa. If we look at what happened in the Zambezi river, the fish populations have been decimated. What makes Vanderkloof unique is that we are dealing with a red listed species, it is a threatened and protected species. There are various other ways of setting up a sustainable fishery. They could choose numerous other venues to do the exploratory phase of this project on..”

PTC: “Gill nets are also called the walls of death. Mesh shaped and available in various sizes, they can be spanned across vast areas. Now when the fish swims into the net, the mesh cuts into its gills like dental floss and this causes the fish to suffocate or drown. This is a replica of a Largemouth Yellow fish, but it can take them up to 12 years to grow to this size”

VO: In 2019 the project was suspended after Gary Shun King presented evidence to the Science faculty that the project had been catching undersized fish for more than five months, which meant it was violating its own permit conditions.

However Rhodes says the project wasn’t suspended as a result of the complaint – the permit expired. And it was always supposed to include fish of all sizes…which was later corrected.

VO: The local fishermen say the project exploited their dire circumstances so that the University Fisheries Department could obtain state funding. For government money to be dispensed the project had to prove that it would benefit the community.

SUPER@ LORENZO DAMSTER, LOCAL FISHERMAN
“They used our names to get some money and when the government sees that it’s a community sustainability project, they go in like that so they can get to that point. As I see it, in the last five years, nothing has changed, the fishermen haven’t changed….it is only about making money for the project so the government can see they are making profit.

VO: Lorenzo Damster represents the Petrusville fishing community on the Advisory Group and says Rouhani and Sauer did not listen to a number of suggestions from the fishermen. The Advisory Group would meet regularly…and Damster says tensions regularly reached boiling point.

VO: The fishermen wanted the project to buy the fish from them for research purposes, which would have created a direct market and generated employment. Instead, the project started selling the fish to the fishermen who then had to take it to the market.

SUPER@ LORENZO DAMSTER, LOCAL FISHERMAN
“We are not even supposed to buy the fish from you. You were supposed to be giving the fish to the fishermen”

VO: On top of this, the project itself was also taking large volumes of fish directly to the market, using the project’s vehicle, trailers, containers and ice machines, while the fishermen had to hitchhike with their fish to get to the market. Rhodes says while some fish was sold, a third of the fish was also donated.

Damster said he fought Rhodes’s project leaders on this point from the start, but they insisted the fish be sold at over R17 per kilogram, a price the impoverished fishermen could not afford.

SUPER@ CLARENS OLIPHANT, MASIFUNDISE DEVELOPMENT TRUST
“As Masifundise, from the beginning we weren’t really ok with the idea, because we know a fisherman doesn’t have the money to buy the fish.

VO: Clarens Oliphant is a local representative of Masifundise Development Trust, an NGO representing the fishing communities.

SUPER@ CLARENS OLIPHANT, MASIFUNDISE DEVELOPMENT TRUST
“He has to come to the water and collect the fish and sell. It is a way of having a little income.”

Rhodes said in their reply that the fishermen suggested the price themselves.

VO: Damster says he was often at loggerheads with the project leaders.

SUPER@ LORENZO DAMSTER, LOCAL FISHERMAN
“It’s the questions I asked, I asked too much about the money, how they control the money how does it work, how can the money not come to the fishermen? The money must help the fishermen”

VO: On a question about the auditing of the funds, Rhodes stated that they are under contract of Northern Cape government and therefore do not have the right to furnish us with any detail related to their funding and referred us to the Northern cape government.

PTC: “I first reached out to the project leaders at Rhodes university in June to establish why the very fishermen that the project claims to want to uplift are the ones feeling that they are being ignored.”

VO: Fishermen say that although they are not opposed to the state-funded project, they don’t feel it is managed in the right way.

SUPER@ ELISE NEL, FORMER PROJECT EMPLOYEE
“They pulled out, all of them pulled out. They were unhappy, they hated Rhodes, they thought Rhodes were taking away their livelihood…they were angry at Rhodes for what they were doing. I didn’t see it at that stage I thought we were trying to help them. But only later on did I realize, these guys are right, we were taking away their livelihood”

PTC: “After decades of working in corporate Johannesburg as an executive assistant, Elize Nel moved to the town of Petrusville. She was one of the first locals to be employed by the project and she says the fishermen became her friends. But it was only months into the project that she started to notice worrying lapses in the project’s management.”

SUPER@ ELISE NEL, FORMER PROJECT EMPLOYEE
“…They were also very excited and as we went along, they started falling off and started to complain about the size of the fish and the market and the fact that we were not including them.

VO: Nel says that in the first couple of months of the project, fish were caught, but no research data was collected.

SUPER@ ELISE NEL, FORMER PROJECT EMPLOYEE
“Little things like this made me realize that everything wasn’t above board... I think it was done very quickly, I don’t think it was thought out properly. Seeing that this is a research project, we need to have things in place to track”

VO: Rhodes conceded that data was not fully captured at the start because the initial period on the dam was used for training. But after the training concluded the capturing of data began.

VO: Neither Rouhani nor Sauer agreed to an on-camera interview and offered written responses facilitated by the head of the fisheries department who said the project had caught 70 largemouth yellowfish, of which 62 were released and 8 had died. He insisted that mesh sizes were selected against catching the largemouth yellowfish.

VO: Despite the various objections against the management of the project, government will continue to fund the project for another year.

SUPER@ KISHAN SANKAR, ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS, FORRESTRY AND FISHERIES
“So again, you jump on the fact that it is only gill nets being used?
ANINA: “It doesn’t matter, gill nets are certain death for an endangered species and government is allowing this?”
“You need to understand that research is going to inform appropriate gear type for decision making”

VO: DAFF says research into commercial viability of a fishery at Vanderkloof dam will continue and disputes that the fishermen are not buying fish from the project.

SUPER@ SUPER@ KISHAN SANKAR, ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS, FORRESTRY AND FISHERIES
“Again, the information coming to you may not be as accurate. We were informed that the fishers were buying from the project and have been many examples of this.
ANINA: “Don’t you think that the best people to tell you that they are not buying the fish, are the fishermen themselves?
“Well if you spoken to them and you have got that information, then you got it”

VO: Although various requests were made to Rhodes university to share the research data collected since 2018, they said no research data can be revealed before the project concludes. They are hoping to complete the research at the end of 2020.

Hier – kan enige plek wees??? VO: Rhodes says the fisherman were part of the design of the project and were consulted at every turn.




VO: Government says the Vanderkloof project serves as blueprint to inform their decision on whether inland fisheries across the country will be viable.

SUPER@ GARY SHUN KING, ICHTHYOLOGIST
“Using a gill net in my opinion is a fatal flaw of this project, if it is proven to be successful, this will mean the end of our inland fisheries.

END.

But only later on did I realize, these guys are right, we were taking away their livelihood” PTC: “After decades of working in corporate Johannesburg as an executive assistant, Elize Nel moved to the town of Petrusville. She was one of the first locals to be employed by the project and she says the fishermen became her friends. But it was only months into the project that she started to notice worrying lapses in the project’s management.” SUPER@ ELISE NEL, FORMER PROJECT EMPLOYEE “…They were also very excited and as we went along, they started falling off and started to complain about the size of the fish and the market and the fact that we were not including them. VO: Nel says that in the first couple of months of the project, fish were caught, but no research data was collected. SUPER@ ELISE NEL, FORMER PROJECT EMPLOYEE “Little things like this made me realize that everything wasn’t above board... I think it was done very quickly, I don’t think it was thought out properly. Seeing that this is a research project, we need to have things in place to track” VO: Rhodes conceded that data was not fully captured at the start because the initial period on the dam was used for training. But after the training concluded the capturing of data began. VO: Neither Rouhani nor Sauer agreed to an on-camera interview and offered written responses facilitated by the head of the fisheries department who said the project had caught 70 largemouth yellowfish, of which 62 were released and 8 had died. He insisted that mesh sizes were selected against catching the largemouth yellowfish. VO: Despite the various objections against the management of the project, government will continue to fund the project for another year. SUPER@ KISHAN SANKAR, ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS, FORRESTRY AND FISHERIES “So again, you jump on the fact that it is only gill nets being used? ANINA: “It doesn’t matter, gill nets are certain death for an endangered species and government is allowing this?” “You need to understand that research is going to inform appropriate gear type for decision making” VO: DAFF says research into commercial viability of a fishery at Vanderkloof dam will continue and disputes that the fishermen are not buying fish from the project. SUPER@ SUPER@ KISHAN SANKAR, ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS, FORRESTRY AND FISHERIES “Again, the information coming to you may not be as accurate. We were informed that the fishers were buying from the project and have been many examples of this. ANINA: “Don’t you think that the best people to tell you that they are not buying the fish, are the fishermen themselves? “Well if you spoken to them and you have got that information, then you got it” VO: Although various requests were made to Rhodes university to share the research data collected since 2018, they said no research data can be revealed before the project concludes. They are hoping to complete the research at the end of 2020. Hier – kan enige plek wees??? VO: Rhodes says the fisherman were part of the design of the project and were consulted at every turn. VO: Government says the Vanderkloof project serves as blueprint to inform their decision on whether inland fisheries across the country will be viable. SUPER@ GARY SHUN KING, ICHTHYOLOGIST “Using a gill net in my opinion is a fatal flaw of this project, if it is proven to be successful, this will mean the end of our inland fisheries. END.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A fishing scheme posing as a research project by Rhodes University at Vanderkloof Dam, is causing the further extinction of the Large Mouth Yellow fish and impoverishing the local fishing community
metadata.Unique Selling Point: A dubious fishing project spearheaded by Rhodes University and funded with taxpayer’s money, is causing the extinction of the critically endangered Large Mouth Yellow fish in their last remaining habitat in Africa, the Vanderkloof dam. The local impoverished fishing community around the dam that has been dependent on fishing for nearly half a century is also further being deprived of resources by the Rhodes project.
metadata.Summary: A suspicious experimental fishing project at Vanderkloof dam, designed to assess the viability of a small-scale fisheries, is slowly causing the extinction of the globally endangered Large Mouthed Yellow fish (LMY). This, while the project that was designed to uplift the poor Northern Cape fishing communities, is now further impoverishing them. The state funded project implemented by Rhodes University seems to be a commercial operation under the guise of research. Tons of fish have been killed and no research data is being furnished to justify the project. The project is also adding to the collapse of the local tourism industry due to the use of illegal gillnets on South Africa’s second largest dam.
metadata.Further information: The Large Mouthed Yellow fish is only found in the Orange and Vaal Systems but due to high level pollution in the Vaal river and dam, Vanderkloof dam is the last remaining habitat for this critically endangered species. Vanderkloof dam is also the bread and butter of the local fishing community. And yet, aware of these issues, Rhodes University has been granted permits by the Northern Cape department of Rural development, exempting them to use illegal gill nets in the dam for alleged research purposes. The project is now depleting the dam of its natural resources while there seems to be no control over the catch and killing of the Large Mouth Yellow fish. Since the project is facilitated by an academic institution, ethical clearance needs to be granted by the university involved to minimize risk to both human and animal involved during data collection. No ethical clearance was obtained at the onset of the project. When it started, the project made lavish promises to the desperately poor fishing communities around the dam who have been surviving on the fish resources for half a century. Since the project is funded by taxpayer’s money, it also committed to skills development for the fishermen. Various fishing methods were also to be explored in order to identify the best possible options when establishing a commercial fishery. After the experiment and skills development, the project was earmarked to be handed over to the local community. Yet, more than two years into the project, the same methods of fishing, which include the use of illegal gill nets, are still being used. The community is forced to buy the fish from the project and sell to the same markets to which the project also sells, at a discounted rate. The local fishermen have not benefited from the project at all.
